title: Do Not Burn What You Do Not Know: Reuchlin, the Hebrew Letters, and the Books of the Jews
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pforzheim, the ninth hour after noon
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia, 'Johann Reuchlin' and de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin' give 29 January 1455 and the hour after noon; older reference works, among them the Jewish Encyclopedia, give 22 February 1455. The two dates are not reconciled in anything reached. Pin is the Dominican cloister of Pforzheim, 48.891238, 8.703899, per de.wikipedia, 'Dominikanerkloster Pforzheim'; that article does not identify the cloister with the Schlosskirche St Michael, and the cloister's own church, St Stephan, was destroyed in 1689
stops.campa: Georg Reuchlin keeps the property accounts of the Dominican house at Pforzheim, and at the ninth hour after noon his wife Elissa Erinna Eck bears him a son. The boy learns his first Latin in the cloister school, from friars of the order that will one day open a heresy process against him. He sings well enough that the household of the Margrave of Baden takes him in for the voice alone. Everything the family has rests on the friars' ledgers and on that voice. The town on the Enz has not yet a printing press of its own.
suggested_refs: The Dominican cloister of Pforzheim, where Georg Reuchlin served as Gueterverwalter

stops.name: Freiburg, matriculation at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: the 1470 matriculation at Freiburg is attested on both language editions of the Wikipedia article; the day, 19 May, comes from the dossier crawl and was not independently located in this session. The judgment that Freiburg taught him little is a paraphrase of older biography carried in the article, marked [R]
stops.campa: At fifteen he enters the arts faculty at Freiburg: grammar, rhetoric, logic, the fixed ladder every German student climbs. He takes no degree there. The account that comes down through the older biographers, and that the encyclopaedias still repeat, is that the place taught him little, which is the sort of judgment a man makes about his schooling only long afterward and in print. Whatever he learns there, he is gone within three years, and he leaves with a reputation for Latin rather than for law.
suggested_refs: The Alte Universitaet of Freiburg im Breisgau, Bertoldstrasse

stops.name: Paris, Greek from a Spartan
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia places the Paris journey in 1473 with Basel following in 1474; en.wikipedia orders it differently, giving 1477 for a move from Basel to Paris. The contradiction between the two editions is not resolved here. No month is recorded. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, which uses 48.8566, 2.3522 for Paris
stops.campa: He goes to Paris in the train of Margrave Frederick of Baden, half tutor and half companion, and finds a city where Greek has been taught for three years and no longer at all. Georgios Hermonymos of Sparta, the first man to teach Greek publicly in the city, a copyist who sells manuscripts and lessons together, gives him the alphabet. Johannes Heynlin von Stein, called Johannes a Lapide, takes him into a circle that has just brought the first printing press in France into the Sorbonne. Reuchlin is eighteen.
suggested_refs: Georgios Hermonymos of Sparta, first public teacher of Greek at Paris
The Sorbonne press established by Heynlin and Guillaume Fichet, 1470

stops.name: Basel, the magisterium and the dictionary
stops.date_confidence: the master of arts at Basel in 1477 is attested on both editions. The Vocabularius breviloquus is a separate matter and the dates disagree: de.wikipedia's works list gives 'Basel 1478', en.wikipedia gives a first publication of 1475-76. Both are recorded and neither is preferred. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, which pins Basel at 47.5596, 7.5886
stops.campa: He follows Heynlin over the Rhine to Basel, takes the baccalaureate and then, in 1477, the master of arts. He lectures on Latin and, which almost nobody in Germany does, on Aristotle in Greek. For the schoolboys he compiles a Latin dictionary, the Vocabularius breviloquus, printed at Basel by Johann Amerbach on the usual account, though the two encyclopaedias date the first edition to 1478 and to 1475 or 1476. It goes through edition after edition for the rest of the century. He is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: Vocabularius breviloquus, printed at Basel by Johann Amerbach
The old lecture halls on the Rheinsprung, University of Basel

stops.name: Orleans, the turn to law
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia gives 1478 for the Orleans enrollment; de.wikipedia gives the Orleans period as 1479 to 1481. The coordinate is the historic university quarter of Orleans; the medieval law faculty building is not precisely documented in anything reached
stops.campa: Humanist teaching pays badly and irregularly, and he has no patrimony behind him. He goes to Orleans, where Germans have studied law for two centuries, and reads the civil law for a bachelor's degree. The Greek does not stop; it simply stops being what he intends to live by. He is twenty-three, and he takes the degree. How long he stays is not settled: one encyclopaedia enrols him in 1478, the other gives the whole Orleans period as 1479 to 1481.
suggested_refs: The German nation of the University of Orleans, law faculty

stops.name: Poitiers, the licentiate in civil law
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia gives July 1481 for the licentiate at Poitiers; de.wikipedia gives 14 June 1481. The month is therefore disputed and the day is given by one source only
stops.campa: At Poitiers he takes the licentiate in imperial law, the degree that qualifies a man to plead in the courts and to advise princes. He is twenty-six, with a master of arts from Basel, law degrees from two French universities, and a printed dictionary carrying his name. The date is disputed: the English article gives July 1481, the German the fourteenth of June. Eleven years of schooling end here. He turns for home across France toward a university a count has just founded in a small town on the Neckar, where he has no post waiting.
suggested_refs: The law faculty of the University of Poitiers

segments.name: The Count's Man: Wuerttemberg and the First Italy

stops.name: Tuebingen, taken into Eberhard's service
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia gives a December 1481 arrival; de.wikipedia gives the matriculation as 9 December 1481. The pin is the old town and university precinct at roughly 48.5216, 9.0576; the 48.5202, 9.0523 that circulates in synthesis falls about 450 metres west-southwest of it
stops.campa: He matriculates at Tuebingen meaning to lecture, and Count Eberhard im Bart takes him instead as interpreter, secretary, legal adviser, and envoy. It is not the appointment he came for. It lasts, with one bitter interruption, until the count's death fifteen years later, and it puts a scholar of Greek in the rooms where treaties are drafted and embassies are briefed. The Latin he writes from now on is chancery Latin as often as it is humanist Latin.
suggested_refs: The university founded by Eberhard im Bart at Tuebingen, 1477

stops.name: Florence, second orator on the count's embassy
stops.date_confidence: the 1482 Italian mission with Eberhard im Bart is attested on both Wikipedia editions and in the Catholic Encyclopedia. The month is from the dossier's February dating and was not independently confirmed. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, which pins the Medicean humanist circle at Florence at 43.7757, 11.2544
stops.campa: Two months after entering the count's household he is riding south over the Alps as second orator of an embassy. In Florence he meets Italian philology in its own city, among men who have been reading Plato in Greek since he was a boy singing in a cloister school on the Enz. He is a German lawyer with a Basel magisterium, standing where the recovery of antiquity is a public project paid for by a banking family. He speaks the language well enough that the Italians remark on it.
suggested_refs: The Medicean humanist circle of Florence in the 1480s

stops.name: Rome, the university and the collegiate church
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1482 embassy reached Rome and that its business concerned the separation of the University of Tuebingen from the collegiate church of St George (en.wikipedia; Catholic Encyclopedia). No month is given anywhere reached; April orders the segment. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, which pins Rome at 41.9028, 12.4964
stops.campa: The embassy's business at the curia is money and jurisdiction: prying the new university at Tuebingen loose from the collegiate church of St George, so that its endowment answers to the count rather than to the canons. Reuchlin drafts, argues, and waits in antechambers. He is twenty-seven and the business belongs to the count. He is learning how a case moves through Rome, which offices decide and which merely delay, and how long a German petitioner may be kept standing.
suggested_refs: The collegiate church of St George, Tuebingen, and the endowment of the university

stops.name: Tuebingen, the doctorate and the first marriage
stops.date_confidence: [R]. de.wikipedia dates the doctorate in laws and the first marriage to 1484-85; the wife is identified only as a daughter of Haenslin Mueller, and no marriage contract has been consulted. The two marriages as dated on de.wikipedia overlap incoherently, the first wife dying about 1500 and Anna Decker married 'after 1496'; both dates are reported and the ordering is not asserted. The tradition that the first wife's property, including an estate at Ditzingen, paid for the expensive doctorate is local and genealogical, and Ditzingen's own article makes no mention of Reuchlin
stops.campa: He marries a widow of the Mueller family and is promoted doctor of laws, the two events falling together in the record and, tradition says, connected: her property, which the local genealogies put at Ditzingen, paid for an expensive degree. The tradition rests on nothing but repetition. The German article names her only as a daughter of Haenslin Mueller, and no marriage contract for her has been consulted here. He is thirty, a salaried adviser with a doctorate in civil law and a wife with land.
suggested_refs: The Reuchlin estate at Ditzingen, claimed by local and genealogical tradition and unattested by any surviving contract

stops.name: Florence, the second Italian journey
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia's 1490 entry names only Giovanni Pico della Mirandola: 'Second Italian journey; encountered Pico della Mirandola'. Marsilio Ficino and Angelo Poliziano appear in no 1490 account on either edition and are older-biography embroidery, marked [R]. de.wikipedia supports the Elijah del Medigo strand loosely, saying conversations with del Medigo awoke Reuchlin's interest in Italy in 1490; en.wikipedia's own article on del Medigo mentions Reuchlin nowhere and has del Medigo leaving Italy for Crete about this time, so that encounter is [R] as well. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json
stops.campa: He comes back to Florence in the year Giovanni Pico della Mirandola is under a papal cloud for nine hundred theses that argued no science better proves the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah. The meeting redirects him. What Pico has done in Latin with borrowed Hebrew, Reuchlin decides to do with Hebrew he can read himself. Older biographies put Ficino and Poliziano in the room; the encyclopaedia entries for 1490 name neither. Somewhere in these months he also argues with Elijah del Medigo, an Aristotelian who thinks the Kabbalah being sold to Christians is not the Kabbalah at all.
suggested_refs: Pico della Mirandola, Conclusiones nongentae (1486), theses on magic and Kabbalah
Elijah del Medigo, critic of the Kabbalistic material passing into Christian hands

stops.name: Linz, the emperor's physician teaches him the letters
stops.date_confidence: attested on both editions that at Linz in 1492 Emperor Frederick III ennobled Reuchlin with a coat of arms and that Reuchlin began Hebrew with Jacob ben Jehiel Loans, the emperor's Jewish physician. No month is recorded. The quote is Reuchlin's own Latin as printed at page 3 of De Rudimentis Hebraicis and reproduced in Barham (1843), p.54; Barham supplies no English rendering of the clause
stops.campa: On embassy to the imperial court at Linz he is ennobled and given arms, and he finds something he wants more. Jacob ben Jehiel Loans, physician to Frederick III, a Jew at a Christian emperor's bedside, agrees to teach him Hebrew. Reuchlin is thirty-seven and begins with the alphabet, right to left, like a child. Fourteen years later, in the preface to the grammar that makes Hebrew teachable in Germany, he names his teacher and calls him humane, which is not a word Christian books of that century commonly spend on Jews.
stops.quote: Is [Jekiel Loans] me, supra quam dici queat, fideliter literas Hebraicas primus edocuit.
stops.quote_source: Reuchlin, De Rudimentis Hebraicis, p.3, as printed in Francis Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (London, 1843), p.54
suggested_refs: Jacob ben Jehiel Loans, physician to Emperor Frederick III and Reuchlin's first Hebrew teacher
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.54

stops.name: Basel, the Pentagrammaton
stops.date_confidence: the 1494 Basel publication of De verbo mirifico, its three speakers, and the five-letter construction are attested on both editions. No month is recorded. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json
stops.campa: The book is a dialogue among three men: Sidonius the pagan, Baruchias the Jew, and a Christian called Capnion, which is Reuchlin's own name turned into Greek smoke. Into the four letters of the divine name he inserts a fifth, the letter shin, and reads the result, YHShWH, as the name of Jesus hidden in the name of God since before the world. It is the first work of Christian Kabbalah printed in Germany. Within fifteen years a young Cornelius Agrippa is lecturing on it publicly at Dole.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, De verbo mirifico (Basel, 1494)
heinrich_cornelius_agrippa.journey.json, stop 'Dole, lecturing on De verbo mirifico', 1509

stops.name: Heidelberg, flight after Eberhard
stops.date_confidence: attested on en.wikipedia: '1496: Fled to Heidelberg following Duke Eberhard's death'. Eberhard im Bart died in February 1496. The Neo-Latin comedies Sergius and Henno are attributed to the Heidelberg years on the same article; no month for the flight is recorded
stops.campa: Eberhard im Bart dies in February and his successor's court has no use for the dead man's councillors. Reuchlin leaves Stuttgart quickly and takes service with Philip, Elector Palatine, at Heidelberg, where Bishop Johann von Dalberg keeps the best humanist circle in Germany. He tutors the elector's sons and writes two Latin comedies for the schools, Sergius and Henno, in which a peasant outwits a lawyer. A man who has just lost everything to a change of ruler writes farce.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, Sergius and Henno, Neo-Latin school comedies of the Heidelberg years
The humanist circle of Bishop Johann von Dalberg at Heidelberg

stops.name: Rome, two years with Obadiah Sforno
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia, 'Obadiah ben Jacob Sforno' states that Reuchlin was in Rome during 1498-1500, that Cardinal Domenico Grimani advised him to apply to Sforno, and that Sforno taught him Hebrew across the two years. The span is therefore two years, not the single year that circulates. The report that he also met Aldus Manutius at Venice on this journey appears on none of the pages fetched and is [R]. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json
stops.campa: Elector Philip sends him to Rome, and he stays two years. Cardinal Domenico Grimani, who collects Hebrew manuscripts, points him at Obadiah Sforno, physician and commentator on the Torah, and Sforno teaches him through 1498 and 1499. He buys Hebrew books with whatever he has. Loans gave him the alphabet at Linz six years before; here he reads scripture beside the man who is writing a commentary on it. He is back over the Alps in 1500, with the books.
suggested_refs: Obadiah ben Jacob Sforno, Reuchlin's Roman teacher, and the introduction by Cardinal Domenico Grimani

stops.name: Stuttgart, the trilingual stone
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin' attests the stone: made 1501, carrying Hebrew olam ha-hayyim, Greek ANASTASIS, and a Latin dedication, standing originally in the Stuttgart Dominikanerkloster and moved to the Leonhardskirche in 1955. The pin is the approximate site of the Dominican cloister south of the old town near the Hauptstaetter Strasse, about 48.772, 9.178; the 48.7776, 9.1798 that circulates for this item is the Altes Schloss, a different building
stops.campa: Back in Wuerttemberg under a friendlier regime, he orders his own memorial stone cut while he is forty-six and in health. It carries three alphabets: the Hebrew words olam ha-hayyim, the world of the living; the Greek ANASTASIS, resurrection; and a Latin dedication naming him Phorcensis, the man from Pforzheim, and Capnion. The Hebrew he has had nine years, the Greek since Paris, the Latin since the friars at Pforzheim taught him to read. The stone stands in the Dominican cloister at Stuttgart.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin's trilingual memorial stone of 1501, Stuttgart Dominikanerkloster, now on the choir wall of the Leonhardskirche

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Swabian League bench
stops.date_confidence: attested on both editions that Reuchlin became one of three judges of the Swabian League's supreme court, succeeding Johannes Vergenhans, called Nauclerus; de.wikipedia gives his tenure as 1502-1513, en.wikipedia hedges the start as approximately 1500-1502. The seat of the court is not given in either article: this file's chronology places the appointment at Tuebingen and the geography at Stuttgart, and neither is documented. The pin is the Altes Schloss at Stuttgart and the seat should be read as unlocated
stops.campa: He succeeds his old mentor Johannes Vergenhans, called Nauclerus, as one of three judges of the supreme court of the Swabian League: the standing tribunal of a confederation of princes, prelates, and imperial cities that keeps its own peace by force. For eleven years this is his salary and his public standing. He hears property, feud, and jurisdiction. Neither of the encyclopaedias that record the office says where in Swabia the court actually sat.
suggested_refs: Johannes Vergenhans (Nauclerus), chancellor of Tuebingen, whom Reuchlin succeeded on the Swabian League bench

stops.name: Denkendorf, quarantine without a library
stops.date_confidence: [R]. de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin' says only that, without his own library, he composed his preaching manual De arte praedicandi there; it gives no year, and the article on Kloster Denkendorf does not mention Reuchlin at all. 1502 comes from the dossier crawl and is unconfirmed; June is used to order the segment. Coordinates corrected to 48.692, 9.3152 per de.wikipedia, 'Kloster Denkendorf'; the 48.6362, 9.3005 in circulation lies about six and a half kilometres south-southwest, in open country
stops.campa: Plague drives the household out of the city and up the Neckar to the monastery at Denkendorf, and he arrives without his books. So he writes the one kind of book a man can write from memory: a short manual on how to construct a sermon, the Liber congestorum de arte praedicandi. The Hebrew work waits on shelves he cannot reach, in a city he cannot enter. It is the only period of his adult life in which he is recorded as writing without a library, and neither the German article on the monastery nor any other page consulted records the year it happened.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, Liber congestorum de arte praedicandi, written in quarantine at Denkendorf

stops.name: Pforzheim, De rudimentis Hebraicis
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia calls the 1506 grammar epoch-making; de.wikipedia, 'Thomas Anshelm' lists 'Rudimenta hebraica (1506)' among Anshelm's output at Pforzheim. No month is recorded. Anshelm's shop address is not documented in anything reached, so the pin is the town, at the corrected Pforzheim coordinate
stops.campa: In the town where he was born, Thomas Anshelm sets Hebrew type running right to left, cut for the purpose, and prints three books in one: a grammar, a lexicon, and a set of exercises. It is the first substantial Hebrew grammar produced by a Christian for Christians in Germany. Anshelm's list for that year gives it as Rudimenta hebraica. Reuchlin pays a large part of the cost himself and it sells slowly. He is fifty-one. Fourteen years earlier he could not read a letter of it.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, De rudimentis Hebraicis libri III (Pforzheim: Thomas Anshelm, 1506)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Judengasse emptied
stops.date_confidence: attested that Maximilian I issued a mandate in 1509 authorizing confiscation of Jewish books hostile to Christianity following Johannes Pfefferkorn's campaign, and that confiscations began in Frankfurt and other Rhineland communities. The September dating and the role of Kunigunde of Austria in obtaining the mandate come from the Bodian teaching page at laits.utexas.edu
stops.campa: Johannes Pfefferkorn, a butcher who converted from Judaism and has been publishing against the community he left, obtains an imperial mandate authorizing the seizure of Jewish books hostile to the Christian faith. He walks into the Frankfurt synagogue with the paper in his hand and carries the books out. The same happens along the Rhine. Reuchlin is not consulted, is not present, and has never met the man. He is a judge of the Swabian League, away south in Wuerttemberg, with a Hebrew library of his own.
suggested_refs: Johannes Pfefferkorn's imperial mandate of 1509 and the seizures in the Frankfurt Judengasse
Miriam Bodian, teaching materials on the Reuchlin-Pfefferkorn controversy, laits.utexas.edu

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Ratschlag
stops.date_confidence: attested on both editions: Reuchlin submitted his commissioned opinion to Emperor Maximilian I on 6 October 1510, arguing against wholesale destruction of Jewish religious and scholarly literature. The place of composition is given as Stuttgart in the dossier and the opinion was submitted to an imperial commission; the pin is the ducal court at the Altes Schloss. The Mutianus quotation is Barham's English
stops.campa: The emperor, having authorized the seizures, asks a commission whether the books should be taken, abolished, and burned. Reuchlin is one of those asked. He answers by sorting: the Talmud, the commentaries, the grammars, the philosophy, the poetry are not blasphemy and are the property of imperial subjects who cannot be robbed without a hearing; anything actually blasphemous must be proved so, book by book, in a court. He recommends instead that the empire endow two chairs of Hebrew for ten years. Not everyone in his own camp admires the performance.
stops.quote: Our friend Reuchlin's opinion aims as much at the renown of the author as at the general benefit; besides the purpose of bringing forward arguments, there transpires throughout a wish to appear learned.
stops.quote_source: Conrad Mutianus Rufus, letter to Urbanus on Reuchlin's Ratschlag, as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.134
suggested_refs: Reuchlin's Ratschlag of 6 October 1510, the commissioned opinion on the confiscation of Jewish books
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.134

stops.name: Tuebingen, the Augenspiegel off Anshelm's press
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia, 'Augenspiegel (Reuchlin)' states the work was printed in autumn 1511 at Tuebingen by Thomas Anshelm and published in German at the Frankfurt autumn book fair, and confirms the motto verbatim. The earlier hedge that the printing place was merely presumed can be dropped. The exact day is not given
stops.campa: Pfefferkorn answers the Ratschlag with a pamphlet called the Handspiegel, the hand mirror, accusing Reuchlin of ignorance of Hebrew and of having been bribed by Jews. Reuchlin replies in German rather than Latin, so that anyone at the Frankfurt fair can read it, prints his suppressed imperial opinion in full inside it, and calls it the Augenspiegel, the eyeglass. Thomas Anshelm, who cut his Hebrew type five years earlier, sets it in Tuebingen in the autumn. One line of it outlives the whole quarrel.
stops.quote: verbrennt nicht, was ihr nicht kennt!
stops.quote_source: Reuchlin, Augenspiegel (Tuebingen: Thomas Anshelm, autumn 1511), quoted verbatim in de.wikipedia, 'Augenspiegel (Reuchlin)'
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, Augenspiegel (Tuebingen: Thomas Anshelm, 1511), published at the Frankfurt autumn fair
Pfefferkorn, Handspiegel (1511)

stops.name: Cologne, the faculty finds heresy
stops.date_confidence: attested that Cologne's theological faculty identified allegedly heretical propositions in the Augenspiegel and that imperial restriction of the book followed in 1512 (en.wikipedia; Encyclopaedia Judaica via jewishvirtuallibrary.org). No month is given. The Pirckheimer letter is dated 1511 by Barham and is placed here for the pressure it answers
stops.campa: The Dominicans of Cologne and the theological faculty of its university go through the Augenspiegel and pull out propositions they call heretical, scandalous, and favourable to Jews. Cologne is the largest city in the empire and its faculty has a long habit of being obeyed. Reuchlin is a sixty-year-old judge with no religious order behind him and no university chair. His friends begin writing to him, and they are already writing about defending a reputation rather than winning an argument.
stops.quote: I hear that some annoyance disturbs thee; but thou who art so adorned with virtue and knowledge, thou needest not be so easily frightened. Believe me confidently, no one can so soon obscure thy fame and thy honour; endure then with a firm mind these affronts from thy foes, and despise their machinations. Virtue is always exposed to the envy of sycophants.
stops.quote_source: Willibald Pirckheimer, letter to Reuchlin (1511), as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.133
suggested_refs: The condemned propositions extracted from the Augenspiegel by the theological faculty of Cologne
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.133

stops.name: Stuttgart, the book taken and the bench given up
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia dates the imperial order temporarily confiscating the Augenspiegel to 7 October 1512; de.wikipedia dates Reuchlin's resignation from the Swabian League judgeship to January 1513. Two events three months apart are narrated at one pin because the seat of the League court is not documented anywhere reached. The Pirckheimer Latin is Barham's, with his English gloss
stops.campa: On the seventh of October an imperial order takes the Augenspiegel out of circulation across the empire. Three months later he gives up the judgeship he has held for eleven years, the office that paid him and placed him. He is nearly fifty-eight, without a post, with his book confiscated and a faculty of theologians assembling a heresy case against him in the largest city in Germany. The advice reaching him from Nuremberg is that answering his accusers at all is beneath him.
stops.quote: Cum tu taces, pro te veritas loquitur
stops.quote_source: Willibald Pirckheimer to Reuchlin, 'be thou silent, and truth shall speak for thee', quoted in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.146
suggested_refs: The imperial order of 7 October 1512 restricting the Augenspiegel
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.146

stops.name: Mainz, summoned within six days
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: en.wikipedia, 'Jacob van Hoogstraten' states that on 15 September 1513 Hoogstraten, as inquisitor, summoned Reuchlin to appear within six days before the ecclesiastical court of Mainz. The venue of the summons is Mainz specifically; Cologne is the seat of Hoogstraten and of the condemning faculty and is a separate strand. The Defensio quotation is Barham's translation, with Barham's wording 'the Colognese' rather than the 'the Cologne people' that circulates
stops.campa: Jacob van Hoogstraten, prior of the Cologne Dominicans and inquisitor for three provinces, summons him to answer before the ecclesiastical court at Mainz within six days. Reuchlin, who has spent eleven years on a bench himself, attacks the jurisdiction and the judge's impartiality rather than the charge, and prints his Defensio contra calumniatores suos Colonienses, addressed to the emperor. Six days is the whole of the notice given. The Defensio ends with a threat dressed up as a courtesy.
stops.quote: Some will blame me for having dealt too mildly with these people, but I promise them to reserve the stripes which the Colognese do not receive now for the other check, if they rage against me again.
stops.quote_source: Reuchlin, closing words of Defensio contra Calumniatores Coloniensis (1513), as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.145
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, Defensio contra calumniatores suos Colonienses (1513)
Jacob van Hoogstraten, inquisitor of Cologne
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.145

stops.name: Speyer, acquitted in the bishop's court
stops.date_confidence: attested verbatim: en.wikipedia, 'Jacob van Hoogstraten' records that on 29 March 1514 the Bishop of Speyer announced that the Augenspiegel contained nothing injurious to the Catholic faith; de.wikipedia has the commission going jointly to the bishops of Worms and Speyer. Coordinates corrected to Speyer Cathedral at 49.3172, 8.4424 per en.wikipedia, 'Speyer Cathedral'; the 8.4325 in circulation lies about 720 metres west of the cathedral. The German ADB places part of Reuchlin's legal defence activity at Augsburg in the same period and does not mention Mainz at all, an unresolved divergence recorded here and not adjudicated
stops.campa: The case is pulled out of Hoogstraten's hands and given to a commission under the bishop of Speyer, or, on the German account, to the bishops of Worms and Speyer jointly. On the twenty-ninth of March the tribunal announces that the Augenspiegel contains nothing injurious to the Catholic faith, acquits its author, and assesses the costs against the inquisitor who brought the charge. It is a clean judicial victory in a bishop's court. Hoogstraten appeals to Rome the same year.
suggested_refs: The Speyer commission of 1514 and its award of costs against Hoogstraten
de.wikisource, ADB entry placing part of the 1513-1514 defence at Augsburg

stops.name: Paris, the theologians condemn the book
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives '1514 (August): University of Paris condemned Augenspiegel'. No day is recorded. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json. The Vadianus letter is undated in Barham and is placed here for its subject
stops.campa: Five months after Speyer clears him, the theological faculty of Paris formally condemns the Augenspiegel, and Cologne, Louvain, Erfurt, and Mainz add their own adverse opinions. The universities of Latin Christendom are voting, one after another, on a German lawyer's German pamphlet about whether Hebrew books may be burned. He never appears before any of them, is never asked what he meant, and cannot appeal a faculty opinion because a faculty opinion is not a judgment. Letters come the other way too, from men who read the argument instead of the verdict.
stops.quote: It is indeed honourable to thee to take the part of the persecuted, but disgraceful to him who, when his arguments for persecution are overthrown, turns against the man who defended him. I fully agree in the principles thou hast expressed in thine apology, for to destroy by fire what might be opposed by intellect and reasoning is by no means a token of a wise man, who relies on the sure foundation and certainty of our faith.
stops.quote_source: Joachim Vadianus, letter to Reuchlin, as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), pp.133-134
suggested_refs: The condemnation of the Augenspiegel by the theological faculty of Paris, August 1514
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), pp.133-134

stops.name: Stuttgart, the letters of obscure men
stops.date_confidence: the Epistolae obscurorum virorum are attested in the general narrative of the affair on both editions, principally attributed to Crotus Rubeanus with Ulrich von Hutten behind the second series; no dedicated page on the satire was pulled in this research and the printing place is disputed. 1515 is the conventional date for the first series. The stop is placed where Reuchlin was rather than where the satire was printed. The Hutten letter quoted is dated 1517 from Bologna by Barham
stops.campa: An anonymous collection of letters begins circulating, written in deliberately atrocious Latin by imaginary Cologne theologians to one another, asking whether it is a mortal sin to eat an egg containing a chick and reporting that Reuchlin has been beaten in argument again. The joke is that they condemn themselves in their own grammar. Crotus Rubeanus is behind the first series and Ulrich von Hutten behind the second. Reuchlin, who is defending himself in earnest before real tribunals, has acquired a party, and the party has decided the way to win is ridicule.
stops.quote: My zeal for thee is sufficiently rewarded by my being able to call myself thy friend, and a Reuchlinist; only be of good courage, the greater part of thy burden rests already on our shoulders, I will continually fan the flame, and I hope it will break out vehemently. Do thou repose while I gather together troops whose age and circumstances fit them for the battle.
stops.quote_source: Ulrich von Hutten, letter to Reuchlin from Bologna, 1517, as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.176
suggested_refs: Epistolae obscurorum virorum, first series 1515, second series 1517
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.176

stops.name: Rome, the case suspended
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia gives 'July 1516: Case quashed by papal court in Rome' and the Jewish Encyclopedia has the Lateran Council deciding in Reuchlin's favour in 1516, but en.wikipedia, 'Jacob van Hoogstraten' describes the same moment as the pope postponing the trial indefinitely. Quashed is too strong: this is a suspension favourable to Reuchlin in practice and not an acquittal on the merits, which is precisely what leaves room for the reversal of 1520. Reuchlin himself is not in Rome. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json
stops.campa: Hoogstraten has appealed the Speyer defeat to Rome, and a papal commission sitting alongside the Fifth Lateran Council hears the matter at length. In July the majority is reported to favour Reuchlin, and Leo X ends the proceedings by imposing silence on both parties rather than ruling. It reads in Germany as a victory and it is written down as one. What has actually happened is that a trial has been postponed without limit. Reuchlin is sixty-one and has not set foot in Italy for eighteen years.
stops.quote: Many princes take thy part, for they honour thee as the father of Greek and Hebrew literature; to the number belong our excellent Bishop of Strasburg, the Elector of Bavaria, together with their courtiers, and a great army of knights.
stops.quote_source: Johann Huttichius, letter to Reuchlin, as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.184
suggested_refs: The papal commission of 1514-1516 and the mandatum de supersedendo of July 1516
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.184

stops.name: Hagenau, De arte cabalistica
stops.date_confidence: the 1517 publication, the three-day dialogue among Simon the Kabbalist, Philolaus the Pythagorean, and Marranus the Muslim, and the dedication to Leo X are attested on both editions. The Hagenau printing place, and whether Anshelm's press had moved there by 1517, is [R]: it comes from the dossier and was not independently verified. No month is recorded. The Pirckheimer passage is from the preface to his Lucian, dedicated to Hieronymus Emser
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after De verbo mirifico he publishes the mature book: three men talking over three days in Frankfurt, a Jewish Kabbalist, a Pythagorean, and a Muslim, on the sefirot, the divine names, and the permutation of letters. He dedicates it to Leo X, the pope whose commission suspended the case against him the year before. It is the fullest account of the Kabbalah available in Latin, and the Hebrew in it was learned from two Jewish teachers, Loans at Linz and Sforno at Rome.
stops.quote: As thou formerly didst look upon me as general in the tumult of war, so must thou now consider me as leading the army in the camp of the Reuchlinists; I neither can nor will keep back, but with thee, who art thyself a chief among the Reuchlinist troops, will I abide the combat: we will not only quietly endure the bitings of sycophants, we will despise and laugh at them.
stops.quote_source: Willibald Pirckheimer, preface to his translation of Lucian, dedicated to Hieronymus Emser, as translated in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), p.172
suggested_refs: Reuchlin, De arte cabalistica libri tres (Hagenau, 1517), dedicated to Pope Leo X
Martin and Sarah Goodman, trans., On the Art of the Kabbalah (Nebraska, 1993), with introductions by G. Lloyd Jones and Moshe Idel

stops.name: Stuttgart, word of the ninety-five theses
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The remark is widely attributed to Reuchlin on hearing of Luther's theses and circulates through twentieth-century compilations rather than any primary letter; no contemporary document carrying it was traced in this research. The date is used only to order the segment against Luther's letter of 31 October 1517
stops.campa: News comes out of Saxony that an Augustinian at Wittenberg has published ninety-five propositions against indulgences and that Rome is displeased. Reuchlin has been the empire's most conspicuous suspected heretic for six years, has an inquisitor's appeal pending against him, and is sixty-two. The remark attributed to him is not documented in any surviving letter, and it is the one sentence of his that everybody quotes. He himself will never follow Martin Luther out of the Roman church.
stops.quote: Thanks be to God, at last, they have found a man who will give them so much to do that they will be compelled to let my old age end in peace.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Reuchlin on receiving news of Luther's theses, 1517; circulated through secondary compilations, no primary source traced
suggested_refs: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and the letter to Albert of Mainz, 31 October 1517

stops.name: Stuttgart, the great-nephew sent to Wittenberg
stops.date_confidence: attested that Reuchlin was appointed to a chair of Hebrew and Greek at Wittenberg in 1518 and sent Melanchthon instead (en.wikipedia). The chair Melanchthon actually took was Greek: en.wikipedia, 'Philip Melanchthon' states he became professor of Greek at Wittenberg in 1518, aged twenty-one, on his great-uncle's recommendation. The kinship is confirmed, Melanchthon's grandmother Elizabeth Reuter being Reuchlin's sister. The stop is placed at Stuttgart, where Reuchlin was; he never travelled to Wittenberg. August orders the segment against Melanchthon's arrival
stops.campa: Wittenberg offers him a chair of Hebrew and Greek. He is sixty-three, under appeal in Rome, and declines it, and puts forward instead his sister's grandson Philipp Schwartzerdt, whom he raised, taught, and renamed by turning the black earth of the German surname into Greek. Melanchthon goes north at twenty-one and takes the Greek chair. Within a year he is Martin Luther's closest colleague and the chief architect of Protestant schooling in Germany.
suggested_refs: The Leucorea at Wittenberg, 51.864722, 12.650278, where Melanchthon took the Greek chair in 1518
martin_luther.journey.json, stop 'Wittenberg, the grave beneath the pulpit', where Melanchthon gives the Latin oration in 1546 and is buried beside Luther in 1560

stops.name: Rome, Leo X reverses himself
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives '1520 (23 June): Pope Leo X condemned Augenspiegel'. Reuchlin is not in Rome; the judgment is delivered in his absence. Coordinates inherited byte-identically from giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json
stops.campa: Four years after suspending the case in his favour, the same pope condemns the Augenspiegel as scandalous and offensive and favourable to Jews, imposes perpetual silence on its author, and orders him to pay the costs of the process. Nothing in the book has changed. What has changed is that Germany now contains an actual heretic, and the curia has no appetite for a second lenient verdict on a German professor. Reuchlin is sixty-five and liable for the costs. He is not imprisoned, not tried criminally, and not required to recant anything he wrote in Hebrew.
suggested_refs: The bull of 23 June 1520 condemning the Augenspiegel

stops.name: Stuttgart, war, famine, and the death of Anna
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia records that Stuttgart in 1519 saw famine, civil war, and pestilence; the Swabian League conquered Wuerttemberg that year. de.wikipedia dates the death of his second wife Anna Decker to about 1519, and dates the marriage itself only to 'after 1496', which cannot be reconciled with the first wife's death about 1500. Both dates are reported and no ordering of the two marriages is asserted here. June orders the segment
stops.campa: The Swabian League, on whose bench he sat for eleven years, conquers Wuerttemberg and drives out its duke. The city he has lived in on and off since 1481 gets war in it, then robbery, then famine, then plague, in that order and inside a single year. Anna Decker, his second wife, dies. He is sixty-four, under a pending appeal at Rome, liable for the costs of his own trial, and alone in a town being fought over by an army he used to serve. He packs the Hebrew library he spent thirty years buying and goes east into Bavaria.
suggested_refs: The Swabian League's conquest of Wuerttemberg, 1519

stops.name: Ingolstadt, arrival in November
stops.date_confidence: attested that Reuchlin reached Ingolstadt by November 1519 after fleeing Stuttgart (en.wikipedia narrative of 1519; ADB corroborates the flight and the Ingolstadt professorship that follows). The day is not recorded
stops.campa: He reaches Ingolstadt in November, a refugee of sixty-four with crates of books and no position. The university here is Catholic and about to become the sharpest anti-Lutheran faculty in the empire, and it takes in a man whose case is still on appeal at Rome. Nobody in Bavaria appears to think this a contradiction, or if they do, no one writes it down. Duke Wilhelm IV spends the winter arranging terms for him, and the chair he will hold does not exist yet. He has no position at all until February.
suggested_refs: The old university of Ingolstadt on the Hohe Schulstrasse

stops.name: Ingolstadt, the Hebrew chair at sixty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 'February 1520: Appointed professor of Hebrew at University of Ingolstadt'; de.wikipedia confirms a well-paid chair secured by Duke Wilhelm IV and a large audience. The day is not recorded
stops.campa: Duke Wilhelm IV gives him a well-paid chair in Hebrew and Greek, and the hall fills past what the faculty expected. He is sixty-five and teaching the alphabet he began learning at thirty-seven from a Jewish physician at an emperor's court, to a room of Bavarian students who can buy his grammar in a shop. Four months into the lectures the bull condemning the Augenspiegel is issued at Rome, imposing silence on him and charging him the costs. He keeps lecturing. Nobody at Ingolstadt appears to have raised it.
suggested_refs: De rudimentis Hebraicis in use as the teaching text of the Ingolstadt Hebrew lectures

stops.name: Tuebingen, the last professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 'Spring 1521: Returned to Tuebingen as professor of Hebrew and Greek'; the reason given for leaving Ingolstadt, plague, is probable rather than documented. April orders the segment
stops.campa: Plague, probably, drives him out of Ingolstadt, and he goes back to the university he first matriculated at forty years earlier hoping to teach, and where a count took him for a secretary instead. He gets the chair at last, in Hebrew and Greek, at sixty-six. In the opinion of 1510 he had told the emperor to endow two chairs of Hebrew in the empire and to keep them ten years, and the emperor had not. He is now teaching in the second such chair of his own life, and nobody endowed either one.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin's 1510 recommendation of two imperial chairs of Hebrew, in the Ratschlag

stops.name: Liebenzell, the baths
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 'Spring 1522: Visited baths of Liebenzell; contracted jaundice and died'. The early-modern description of the illness, jaundice or yellow fever, does not map onto a modern diagnosis. Coordinates corrected to 48.7742, 8.7314 per de.wikipedia, 'Bad Liebenzell'; the 48.7654, 8.7346 in circulation sits about a kilometre south of the town
stops.campa: In the spring he goes up the Nagold valley to the warm springs at Liebenzell, apparently for his health, which is what the baths are for. He falls ill there instead. The sources call it jaundice, or the yellow fever, a name that in 1522 covers whatever turns a man that colour and does not resolve into any modern diagnosis. He is sixty-seven and has been lecturing at Tuebingen for a year. He does not recover, and the record does not say whether he was carried back down the valley or died where the water was.
suggested_refs: The baths of Liebenzell in the Nagold valley

stops.name: Stuttgart, the thirtieth of June
stops.date_confidence: the date is agreed everywhere; the place is not. Modern consensus gives Stuttgart: en.wikipedia's infobox reads 'Died: 30 June 1522 (aged 67), Stuttgart, Duchy of Wuerttemberg', and de.wikipedia agrees. The nineteenth-century reference works give Liebenzell: the ADB states plainly that he died at Bad Liebenzell, and the Jewish Encyclopedia has him dying 'at Liebenzell, near Hirschau, Wuerttemberg'. This is modern encyclopaedias against nineteenth-century ones, not two coequal traditions, and it is recorded rather than resolved. The pin is the Leonhardskirche, where the burial is not in dispute
stops.campa: He dies on the thirtieth of June, sixty-seven years old, in the year Luther's German New Testament is being set in type at Wittenberg in the town where his great-nephew holds the Greek chair. He is still under the papal order of silence and still liable for the costs. Whether he dies at Stuttgart or at the baths where he took the illness is a question the reference books answer two ways: the modern encyclopaedias say Stuttgart, the nineteenth-century ones say Liebenzell, and nothing consulted here reconciles them.
suggested_refs: The contradiction between en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia on one side and the ADB and Jewish Encyclopedia on the other regarding the place of death

stops.name: Stuttgart, buried in the Leonhardskirche
stops.date_confidence: the burial in the Leonhardskirche beside his second wife Anna is attested on both language editions. No day is recorded; July orders the stop after the death. Coordinates 48.7734, 9.1805 per de.wikipedia, 'Leonhardskirche (Stuttgart)'. The Erasmus quotation is verified in Barham's Appendix I at p.236, not the p.286 that circulates, and is spoken by Brassicanus, not by Pompilius
stops.campa: They lay him in the Leonhardskirche beside Anna. Within months Erasmus, who had defended him carefully and never wholeheartedly, writes a colloquy in which two friends discuss a vision of Reuchlin's reception among the saints, with Jerome coming out to meet him because they had the three languages in common. Erasmus calls the piece the Apotheosis Capnionis, the deification of Capnion. The pope's condemnation of the Augenspiegel is two years old and has not been withdrawn.
stops.quote: That excellent brave man, John Reuchlin, that was well skilled in three languages, is dead.
stops.quote_source: Erasmus, Apotheosis Capnionis, spoken by Brassicanus; English translation in Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), Appendix I, p.236
suggested_refs: Erasmus, Apotheosis Capnionis, the colloquy on Reuchlin's reception among the saints
sources: Barham, The Life and Times of John Reuchlin (1843), Appendix I, p.236

stops.name: Worms, standing on the wall of the Luther monument
stops.date_confidence: attested that Reuchlin appears on the Lutherdenkmal at Worms, and that he is a full standing statue on the monument's surrounding wall rather than a relief: de.wikipedia, 'Lutherdenkmal (Worms)' places him there alongside Melanchthon, Frederick the Wise, and Philip the Magnanimous, with Luther central and Waldes, Wyclif, Hus, and Savonarola below. No date for the figure was established in this research; 1868 is used only to order the posthumous stops and is not asserted
stops.campa: In the city where Luther refused to recant, a bronze company is assembled around him on a stone platform: Waldes, Wyclif, Hus, and Savonarola seated below as forerunners, and standing on the surrounding wall the men who made the thing hold, among them Philipp Melanchthon and, a few paces from his own great-nephew, Johannes Reuchlin. He had refused the Wittenberg chair, refused the break with Rome, and died a Catholic under papal silence. The monument enrolls him anyway.
suggested_refs: The Lutherdenkmal at Worms and the figures on its surrounding wall

stops.name: Stuttgart, the church in ruins and the stone brought back
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Leonhardskirche was severely damaged in the Stuttgart raid of 22 August 1944 and rebuilt 1948-1954 under Rudolf Lempp, and that the gravestone survived and is displayed on the choir wall with an 1871 portrait medallion (de.wikipedia, 'Leonhardskirche (Stuttgart)'). de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin' gives 1955 for the move of the stone into the church; the church's own article dates the rebuilding to 1954 and does not name 1955, an unresolved date contradiction between two pages recorded here and not adjudicated. No day is recorded
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August 1944 the bombing takes the Leonhardskirche down to its walls. The 1501 stone, with its Hebrew world of the living and its Greek resurrection, survives the raid, as does the marble medallion of his face cut in 1871. The rebuilding runs from 1948 to 1954 under Rudolf Lempp, and stone and medallion go up side by side on the choir wall. The German articles give 1955 and 1954 for that installation and have not been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Reuchlin's 1501 memorial stone and the 1871 portrait medallion, choir wall, Leonhardskirche, Stuttgart

stops.name: Pforzheim, the prize on the five-hundredth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia, 'Reuchlinpreis' gives the foundation by the city of Pforzheim in 1955 on the five-hundredth anniversary of his birth, for outstanding German-language humanities scholarship, awarded roughly biennially with the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences, with Gershom Scholem among the laureates in 1969 and Hans-Georg Gadamer in 1971. The 1922 Barlach medal is attested on de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin'; the claim that en.wikipedia carries it is wrong, that article having no commemoration section at all. Scholem's reported remarks in 1969 crediting Reuchlin with helping begin the scholarly study of Judaism are summarized secondhand and the acceptance speech itself was not located, so that attribution is [R]
stops.campa: The four hundredth anniversary of his death, in 1922, had produced a commemorative medal cut by Ernst Barlach. The five hundredth of his birth produces something with a longer reach: the city founds the Reuchlinpreis for German-language scholarship in the humanities, awarded every second year with the Heidelberg Academy. In 1969 it goes to Gershom Scholem, who spent his life on the Jewish Kabbalah that Reuchlin was tried for defending, and in 1971 to Hans-Georg Gadamer.
suggested_refs: The Reuchlinpreis of the city of Pforzheim, founded 1955
Ernst Barlach's commemorative medal of 1922

stops.name: Pforzheim, the Reuchlinhaus in the Stadtgarten
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia, 'Reuchlinhaus' gives construction 1957-1961 to a 1953 design by Manfred Lehmbruck, on the site of an earlier hall of 1900-1945 destroyed in the bombing, now housing the Schmuckmuseum and the Kunstverein. The statue by Matthias Daempfle is placed in the Stadtgarten by de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin', while de.wikipedia, 'Pforzheim' refers to a Reuchlin statue am Schlossberg: an internal conflict within German Wikipedia, recorded and not resolved. The Goethe couplet is traceable to a named text, the Zahme Xenien, book V, and is quoted in full on de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin'; the claim that en.wikipedia carries the Wunderzeichen phrase is wrong
stops.campa: Pforzheim, bombed flat in 1945, rebuilds its city garden over the ruin of the hall that stood there from 1900, and puts up a glass and steel building named for him, designed by Manfred Lehmbruck and finished in 1961. It holds a jewellery museum and an art society and no exhibit about Reuchlin at all. A statue of him by Matthias Daempfle stands in the same park, or on the Schlossberg, depending which German article you read; the two do not agree. What the town actually quotes on him is a rhymed couplet of Goethe's, out of the Zahme Xenien.
stops.quote: Reuchlin! Wer will sich mit ihm vergleichen, zu seiner Zeit ein Wunderzeichen.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Zahme Xenien, book V, quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Johannes Reuchlin'
